entries.sentence: Diverticular disease is a condition in which small pouches in the wall of the large intestine cause symptoms, and diverticulitis is when those pouches become inflamed or infected.
entries.note: NHS: pouches (diverticula) in the bowel wall; diverticulitis = infected or inflamed. NIDDK: disease term used when pouches cause symptoms, bleeding, inflammation or complications.

entries.sentence: Diverticula are small pouches that push outward through weak spots in the wall of the large intestine.
entries.note: NIDDK: small pouches push outward through weak spots in the colon wall.

entries.sentence: Most people develop some as they get older, and few of them ever have symptoms.
entries.note: NHS: most people develop some pouches with age but few have symptoms.

entries.sentence: When the pouches cause symptoms, bleeding or inflammation, doctors use the term diverticular disease.
entries.note: NIDDK: term used when pouches cause symptoms, bleeding, inflammation or complications.

entries.sentence: Diverticulitis, in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe.
entries.note: NHS: diverticulitis = infected/inflamed pouches; NIDDK: most often abdominal pain, usually severe.

entries.sentence: Complications are uncommon but can include a blockage, an abscess or a hole in the bowel.
entries.note: NHS: complications uncommon; blockage, abscess, bowel perforation, occasionally surgery.

entries.sentence: Small pouches form and push outward through weak spots in the wall of the large intestine.
Experts are not sure what causes diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
entries.note: NIDDK: doctors not sure what causes these conditions.

entries.sentence: Diverticulitis happens when the pouches become inflamed or infected.
Getting older
entries.note: NHS: most people develop pouches as they age; NIDDK: age is a major factor.

entries.sentence: A diet low in fibre and high in red meat
Lack of physical activity
Medicines such as NSAIDs and steroids
Obesity
Smoking

entries.note: NIDDK: research suggests certain genes may play a part.

entries.sentence: A high temperature
entries.note: NHS lists high temperature among signs.

entries.sentence: Blood in the stool
In severe illness, signs of sepsis such as confusion or pale, blotchy skin
entries.note: NHS 999 advice lists sepsis signs, confusion, pale or blotchy skin.

entries.sentence: Bleeding
entries.note: NIDDK complications: bleeding, infections, perforations or tears, blockages.

entries.sentence: An abscess in the colon caused by infection
entries.note: NIDDK: infection can form an abscess; NHS lists abscess.

entries.sentence: A hole (perforation) in the bowel
entries.note: NHS: hole in the bowel; NIDDK: perforations or tears.

entries.sentence: A blockage of the bowel
A fistula, an abnormal connection that may need surgery
entries.note: NIDDK: surgery may be recommended for complications such as fistula or intestinal obstruction.

entries.sentence: Diagnosis rests on the person's history, a physical examination and tests.
entries.note: NIDDK: doctors review history and do a physical exam.

entries.sentence: Tests may include a colonoscopy or a CT scan, and blood tests that look for inflammation are commonly used.
entries.note: NIDDK/NHS: colonoscopy or CT scan; NICE evidence review: WBC and CRP commonly used to help diagnose diverticulitis.

entries.sentence: Symptoms of diverticular disease are usually eased with painkillers such as paracetamol, bulk-forming laxatives and antispasmodic medicines.
Antibiotics are used when diverticulitis is caused by infection.
People admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein.
entries.note: NICE NG147: offer IV antibiotics to people admitted to secondary care with suspected complicated acute diverticulitis.

entries.sentence: Surgery to remove part of the colon may be considered for complications such as a fistula or a blockage.
entries.note: NIDDK: colectomy; surgery for fistula or obstruction.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes gradually adding fibre with plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight as helpful steps.
It is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the condition.
entries.note: MedlinePlus: whether low-fibre diet leads to this is not well proven.

entries.sentence: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy rectal bleeding, or signs of sepsis.
NHS 111 or a GP the same day is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, worsening or lasting tummy pain, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.
The word diverticula describes small pouches that form in the wall of the large intestine, which is also called the bowel.
Having the pouches, known as diverticulosis, usually causes no discomfort, and most people with them never notice.
entries.note: NIDDK: most people with diverticulosis have no discomfort or symptoms.

entries.sentence: Sometimes they are found by chance during tests done for another reason.
entries.note: NIDDK: sometimes noticed while performing tests for other reasons.

entries.sentence: Doctors speak of diverticular disease when the pouches lead to symptoms, bleeding, inflammation or complications.
Without inflammation, the disease can cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating.
Diverticulitis is the stage in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, as the NHS describes it.
entries.note: NHS describes diverticulitis as infected or inflamed pouches.

entries.sentence: NIDDK, a United States institute, says experts are not sure what causes these conditions.
It lists factors that may play a part, including genes, and says researchers are still studying changes in gut bacteria and immune problems.
entries.note: NIDDK: genes; microbiome changes and immune problems still studied.

entries.sentence: Diverticulitis most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe.
The NHS lists severe, constant tummy pain and a high temperature among the signs, alongside constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and blood in the stool.
Pain, bloating and bowel changes can also occur with diverticular disease that is not inflamed.
Without inflammation being shown by tests, the diagnosis is not settled by symptoms alone.
entries.note: PMC4789974: diagnosis needs evidence of inflammation, CRP/WBC and localisation by ultrasound or CT.

entries.sentence: Complications are uncommon, according to the NHS.
They can include a blockage, an abscess or a hole in the bowel, and they sometimes need surgery.
NIDDK also lists bleeding, and explains that an infection can form an abscess in the colon.
Pain that is severe or constant, a high temperature, or blood in the stool are the features the NHS highlights when it advises getting medical help.
Doctors start with the person's history and a physical examination.
Tests such as a colonoscopy or a CT scan may then be used to diagnose diverticular disease or diverticulitis.
A NICE evidence review notes that the white blood cell count and C-reactive protein, a blood marker of inflammation, are commonly used to help diagnose diverticulitis and its complications.
entries.note: NICE evidence review: WBC and CRP commonly used.

entries.sentence: A review of diagnosis says the aim is to show inflammation and then to place it at a diverticulum using ultrasound or CT.
The NICE review reports good sensitivity for CT, which means it picks up most true cases.
entries.note: NICE review: good sensitivity for CT; 'picks up most' is a plain-word gloss.

entries.sentence: In an acute illness, blood tests together with CT are described by one review as the gold standard.
entries.note: PMC9793761: laboratory work-up plus CT gold standard in the acute setting.

entries.sentence: Treatment depends on whether the problem is diverticular disease or diverticulitis and on how unwell the person is.
entries.note: NHS separates treatments; NICE separates by systemic illness; inference.

entries.sentence: For diverticular disease, the NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol, bulk-forming laxatives and antispasmodic medicines.
Antibiotics are used when diverticulitis is caused by infection.
NICE guideline NG147 sets out different routes.
People who are unwell all over the body but do not need referral are offered antibiotics by mouth.
entries.note: NICE: for systemically unwell people not meeting referral criteria oral antibiotics are offered.

entries.sentence: For people who are systemically well and have no conditions that raise the risk of infection, the committee noted that watchful waiting is an option.
entries.note: NICE committee noted watchful waiting option.

entries.sentence: Those admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein.
Surgery to remove part of the colon, called a colectomy, may be recommended for complications such as a fistula or a blockage.
NICE recommends against offering antibiotics or an aminosalicylate medicine to prevent diverticulitis from coming back.
entries.note: NICE: do not offer aminosalicylate or antibiotics to prevent recurrent acute diverticulitis.

entries.sentence: The NHS self-care advice includes adding fibre to the diet gradually while drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight.
It also says NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen and opioids such as codeine can cause stomach problems and raise the risk of a bowel perforation.
NIDDK lists a diet low in fibre and high in red meat, little physical activity, NSAIDs and steroids, obesity and smoking as factors that may raise the risk of diverticulitis or its complications.
MedlinePlus suggests a high-fibre, low-red-meat diet and not smoking.
However, it also states that it is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the problem.
NIDDK describes age as a major factor, so lifestyle is only part of the picture.
entries.note: NIDDK: age is a major factor; the conclusion is a cautious summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS says most people develop some pouches as they get older, and that few have symptoms.
Researchers are also still studying the roles of changes in gut bacteria and of immune problems.
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, or being unable to pass stool or wind.
The same applies to heavy bleeding from the back passage and to signs of sepsis, such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin, or abnormal temperature or breathing.
NHS 111 or the GP the same day is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not settling, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.
Fever, severe pain and bleeding can also point towards complications such as an abscess, a blockage or a hole in the bowel, which the NHS says sometimes need surgery.
entries.note: NHS complications and urgent-advice sections; linking of symptoms to complications is a close paraphrase of both.

entries.sentence: The routes named are 999 for emergencies, NHS 111 or the GP the same day for urgent symptoms, and a routine GP appointment otherwise.
No. Diverticulosis means having the small pouches in the wall of the large intestine, which usually causes no symptoms.
Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms or problems.
Diverticulitis is when the pouches become inflamed or infected.
NICE guideline NG147 offers antibiotics by mouth to people who are unwell all over the body but not referred to hospital.
It notes that watchful waiting is an option for people who are systemically well with no conditions that raise infection risk.
People in hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein.
NICE sets these out as recommendations for the clinician to apply to the individual.
The NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol among the treatments for diverticular disease symptoms.
It says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and opioids such as codeine, can cause stomach problems and raise the risk of a bowel perforation.
A pharmacist or GP can advise on the right choice for an individual.
entries.note: General routing; NHS advises seeing doctor.
